1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the extra pawn on e4, so Black has to decide at once how to hold it. White commits to a gambit: a pawn down in return for quick development and open lines, and Black's task is to survive the early initiative and keep the material.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Be3.strategy: Guards d4 and develops, but does not attack the pawn on e4, so there is no pressure on it yet. A quieter way into the gambit that leaves White a free hand over the set-up, though Black gets time to organise the defence of the extra pawn.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Be3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Diemer-Rosenberg Attack

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7, but the bishop does nothing about the extra pawn on e4. Black keeps it and develops freely, while White has created neither the pawn lever nor the piece pressure that make a gambit worth its price.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Bc4.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Fritz Attack

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.strategy: Attacks e4 with the pawn before any piece is out, which takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal. Black strikes back with ...e5: if White takes on e5, the queen trade costs the right to castle, and if White takes on e4, ...exd4 leaves Black a pawn up.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Blackmar Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.background: Its popularity was short-lived, since the gambit was basically unsound: Black secures a superior position with 3...e5.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The natural defence: the knight guards the pawn on e4 and develops towards the centre. Black accepts the gambit and keeps the extra pawn for now, while White gets a lead in development and the chance to open the f-file; Black must neutralise that initiative before the pawn counts.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5.background: Ignatz von Popiel also provided analysis of this countergambit, which was common at the time.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn instead of guarding e4. If White takes on e5, the queens come off and White either loses the right to castle or has to undevelop the knight, so the game heads for a quiet, equal endgame. Black trades the gambit's sting for safety.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Zeller Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Defends the pawn with the bishop and brings it out before ...e6 can shut it in. The pawn on e4 cramps White, since a knight arriving on f3 or a bishop on d3 would be taken by it. White usually attacks the pawn a second time with the f-pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.strategy: Holds the pawn with the f-pawn, but at a price: the e8-h5 diagonal opens, so the white queen can give check on h5, and the kingside is loosened while Black's pieces are still at home. White can first prevent ...e5 and then attack e4 again.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Netherlands Variation
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.background: The name comes from the Dutch Defence, which can also reach this position through 1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once instead of defending the extra pawn. White can push d5 to gain space and keep the knight's pressure on e4, so Black's counterattack soon needs more support than it has. A rarely tested countergambit that leaves Black short of development.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 c5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Reversed Albin Countergambit

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3.strategy: Hits e4 a second time: if Black takes, the queen recaptures with an attack on the bishop and the b7 pawn at once, so Black keeps the pawn only by adding a defender. The price is that the f-pawn takes f3 from the king's knight.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3 Nf6.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Vienna Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3 Nf6.background: Matthias Wahls recommended it in his book Modernes Skandinavisch, where he saw it as a refutation of the Blackmar-Diemer Gambit.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3 Nf6.strategy: Adds a second defender to e4 and brings the knight out, so the pawn is attacked twice and defended twice and White cannot win it back for free. Black keeps the extra pawn in a solid position, and White has to keep paying for the initiative with development.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3 Nf6 5.B.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Zeller Defence, Soller Attack
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3 Nf6 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop with a pointer at f7 and keeps the tension on e4 instead of taking at once. White chooses development over regaining the pawn, which fits the gambit's logic, and Black must still find a way to consolidate the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nxe4.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit, Lange Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with the knight and leaves d4 under fire: Black can take it with the queen, after which White plays for activity and development against a pawn deficit. A sharp, principled choice that keeps the game complicated.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.dxe5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit, Endgame Variation
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.dxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn and invites a queen trade, after which White's king loses castling or the knight has to retreat. White heads for a quiet, equal endgame with few winning chances for either side, a safe choice for those who do not want a sharp gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nge2.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit, Rasmussen Attack
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nge2.strategy: Supports d4 and develops without taking, declining the exchange. But the knight blocks the f1-bishop and the queen's diagonal, and Black develops with gain of time against d4 while keeping the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Be3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit, Soller Attack
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Be3.strategy: Guards d4 and develops, but ignores the extra pawn. Black can take on d4, and when the bishop recaptures the knight attacks it with gain of time, so White has less to show for the gambit than in the lines with direct pressure.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Qh5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Lemberger Countergambit, Sneiders Attack
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5 4.Qh5.strategy: Brings the queen out early and threatens to take on e5, but Black defends the pawn with a developing move that also hits d4. The queen is then a target and White has spent time for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3.strategy: The gambit's defining move: the pawn attacks e4, and if Black takes it White recaptures with a developing move and a half-open f-file. White offers a pawn for speed and attacking chances, and Black has to defend precisely, since inaccuracies are punished quickly.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: von Popiel Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.background: An older idea than Diemer's 4.f3, played by Ignatz von Popiel in 1889.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: Aims at the knight that guards e4: if it is exchanged, Black's pawn structure is damaged and the e4 pawn loses a defender. An older plan than the f-pawn lever, but it lets Black bring a second defender to e4 at once and keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Rasa-Studier Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3.strategy: Develops and covers d4 but does not attack the extra pawn a second time: the knight on f6 holds e4 comfortably, and White gets little of the speed and open lines that justify the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bf5.strategy: Adds a second defender to the e4 pawn and develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, so exchanging the knight does not win the pawn back. Black keeps the extra pawn and accepts a damaged pawn structure for it.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and removes the f-pawn, so Black is a pawn up. White recaptures with a developing move and gets the half-open f-file and a lead in development, which Black has to neutralise carefully; accepting is the principled way to test the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 c6.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: O'Kelly Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 c6.background: Many sources recommend it as a way of reaching the Ziegler Defence by another route.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 c6.strategy: A solid move that backs the d5 square and prepares to develop the bishop outside the pawn chain and play ...e6. It also removes a sharp bishop option that White has when Black captures on f3 first. The extra pawn is kept and the plan is to consolidate.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 Bf5.strategy: Defends the pawn with the bishop and brings it out before ...e6 can shut it in; the e4 pawn is attacked twice and defended twice. The same position arises if Black plays ...Bf5 a move earlier; it is a solid way to meet the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 c5.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Brombacher Countergambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once instead of settling the centre. White can gain space with a pawn push while the e4 pawn is still under pressure, and Black's development lags behind; a risky way to avoid the main line.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 Nc6.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Lamb Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second attacker on d4 with a developing move, but lets White gain space with a pawn push that sends the knight to e5. There it is well placed, yet White keeps the initiative and the e4 pawn is still under pressure; a double-edged line.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e3.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Langeheinicke Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e3.background: Strong players often use it to avoid the complications of 4...exf3 5.Nxf3.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e3.strategy: Gives the pawn back at once to avoid the complications of capturing: White recaptures with the bishop and has a lead in development with the initiative unslowed. Black avoids the sharp lines but is left passively placed and struggles to equalise.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e6.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Weinsbach Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e6.strategy: Returns the pawn and settles for solidity: White simply recaptures on e4, getting a broad centre and a half-open f-file for free, while Black's c8-bishop is blocked behind the e6 pawn. Sound, but it gives White the easier game.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e5.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Elbert Countergambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e5.strategy: Strikes at d4, but White takes on e5 with gain of time: the pawn hits the knight, and after the queen trade it must retreat, so Black has lost the tempo and White wins the e4 pawn back with the better game, even though its king can no longer castle.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 a6.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Gedult Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 a6.strategy: A slow flank move that does nothing about e4: White simply recaptures the pawn on e4 and has a full centre, a half-open f-file and the lead in development. Black has given back the extra pawn and gained nothing for it.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bf5 5..strategy: Trades off the knight that guards e4, leaving that pawn held by the bishop alone and Black with doubled pawns after the recapture. White gives up the bishop for a lasting structural edge and goes after the bishop that holds e4.
Recaptures with the e-pawn, which keeps the pawn cover in front of the castled king on g7 and h7. The pawns on f7 and f6 are doubled, but the extra pawn is intact and the bishop still holds e4.
Kicks the bishop that defends e4 and gains kingside space, but it loosens White's own king's side too. If the bishop gives way, White continues to harass it, since the pawn on e4 depends on it.
Keeps the bishop defending e4 and out of the pawn's reach, so the extra pawn stays. Black has to be ready for the white kingside pawns to keep chasing the bishop, and the doubled f-pawns need care.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e6 5.fx.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Declined: Weinsbach Defence, Pfrang Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 e6 5.fx.strategy: Regains the pawn, builds the pawn centre on e4 and d4 and half-opens the f-file for the rook, while Black's ...e6 has blocked in the c8-bishop. The gambit has become a comfortable lead in space and development.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Recaptures with a developing move and takes over f3, keeping the queen at home. White is a pawn down but has the knight on its best square, a half-open f-file and a lead in development, and aims for a kingside attack.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ryder Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Most of the analysis in Diemer's late-1950s book Vom Ersten Zug An Auf Matt! is devoted to this double-pawn sacrifice.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which hits b7 and f6 at once, and offers the d4 pawn as a second sacrifice for development and attack. There is doubt that the compensation is enough for two pawns, and Black can also decline the offer.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Gunderam Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Gerhart Gunderam analysed it extensively and published his analysis in a book on the Blackmar-Diemer Gambit in 1984.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Develops the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and eyes c2. Black keeps the extra pawn and a sound structure, while White usually sets about harrying the bishop with the knight and kingside pawns.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ziegler Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Diemer tended to name lines after opponents who first played them against him, and this one carries Ziegler's name; most of its theory was established by Gerhart Gunderam. Most modern authors recommend it as Black's antidote to the gambit.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: A quiet, solid move that fixes a sturdy structure and prepares to develop the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain. Black keeps the extra pawn and aims to neutralise the initiative first; it is Black's most reliable set-up against the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Bogoljubow Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Diemer himself played it in a game against Efim Bogoljubow, who answered with 6.Bg5.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to add pressure on d4, especially once ...c5 follows. Black keeps the extra pawn in a compact set-up, and White has to prove the compensation with a precise kingside plan.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Euwe Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: It was analysed by Max Euwe.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Aims for a solid pawn structure with an extra pawn, at the cost of shutting in the c8-bishop. White must prove its compensation, and a second pawn sacrifice has scored well in practice but probably does not give enough.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Teichmann Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Pins the knight to the queen and prepares to trade it, which would remove a defender of d4 and weaken White's hold on the centre. White usually challenges the bishop at once, and the game can turn sharp.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Holwell Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Brings the queen out early to press on d4, but White gains time by attacking it with a minor piece. Black has the extra pawn, but the queen is more exposed than useful and the development lags.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Kaulich Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Strikes at d4 before developing. If White takes on c5, the d-file opens for a queen trade and Black has the pawn to win back, so the gambit's attack is blunted, but Black has spent time on a premature counterstrike.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Pietrowsky Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Adds a second attacker on d4, but the knight can be pinned along the diagonal to the king, because d7 is empty. White gains time with the pin and the lead in development grows.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ritter Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal. A flexible but slow choice: it does not challenge d4 and lets White complete development with its initiative intact.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Schlutter Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Develops the second knight and covers e5 and f6, but it blocks the c8-bishop and the d-file, so Black's pieces still have to untangle while White keeps developing with the initiative.

Centralises the knight on a square from which it covers g4 and g6, two retreat squares of the bishop, and prepares to drive that bishop back with the g-pawn. White keeps the initiative the gambit pawn was paid for, and Black has to handle the bishop with care.

Guards the bishop with a pawn and opens the diagonal for the king's bishop, so that Black can develop and castle while keeping the extra pawn. The knight on e5 stays unchallenged, so Black must expect a kingside pawn advance against the bishop and a lasting initiative for the pawn.

Puts the question to the pinning bishop at once: trade it for the knight or retreat. White welcomes the trade, because the recapture with the queen develops it with an eye on b7, and the two bishops and the lead in development make up for the pawn.

Removes a defender of the d4 pawn and eases the pressure of White's attack by exchanging a piece. After the queen recaptures, d4 is attacked and undefended while b7 is under fire, so each side has a loose pawn to look after. The price is the bishop pair, which White gets.

Pins the f6 knight to the queen, so Black cannot simply carry on developing: the knight that guards the kingside and the centre is tied down until Black unpins. White develops with a threat in view and goes for quick castling and a kingside attack, while Black holds a pawn and a sound pawn structure.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Euwe Defence, Duthilleul Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Brings the bishop out at once to a diagonal pointing at the kingside, but before the pin on the f6 knight that the bishop on g5 would give. Black is then free to pin the c3 knight or to strike at d4 straight away, so White's attack builds more slowly than with the natural pin.

Breaks the pin by putting the king's bishop in front of the queen, and clears the way for castling. It is the natural answer, and Black keeps the extra pawn with a solid structure, but must still withstand the lead in development White has bought with it.

Develops the bishop to its most active square, where it eyes f7, which only the king defends. White accepts being a pawn down for quick development and rapid castling, aiming the pieces at the black king while Black's bishop is not yet in play.

Completes the fianchetto and prepares to castle. The bishop stands behind its own knight for now, but it adds to the pressure on d4 as soon as the knight moves, and a later ...c5 attacks that pawn again. Black aims to keep the extra pawn and hit d4.
